doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: Music and movies aboard the submarine
summary: They played electrical transcriptions and watched Destination Tokyo hundreds of times.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Were you fellas able to follow any of the music scene that was happening in the states while you were overseas?

Oh sure. And we got — I’ll never forget — we got a lot of the electrical transcriptions that the guys did, and boy there’s some wonderful jazz on those things. And it’s too bad they ended up the way they did but we’d get those, I used to play those all the time.
Were those the V-discs, or was that something different?

No, these were big, well they were as big as LPs really. And they were jazz — well you’ve heard Benny Carter and others talk about how they got a bum deal out of it but there’s still a lot of them that are under wraps that you can’t get. But they’d ship those over and lots of them. And we had movies on the submarines. I saw “Destination Tokyo” at least five hundred times.
Did you guys chuckle sometimes at the way the war was portrayed in films?

Oh yes. Yes. We’d watch — that movie in particular was the popular war submarine movie of the time. And we’d set it up in the Forward Torpedo Room, the guys would just sit around and with a little projector you know. And they knew every line. They’d go through it, every single line, the guys would know. And laugh. It was so much bull you know. But they got a kick out of it.
It was a — I’m not sure special is the right word — but it certainly was a significant historical time in this country.
And when you look back on it, I just had seen a promotional film that Jimmy Stewart had done, trying to get pilots. And it worked amazingly well I guess.
People responded to that kind of thing.
Yeah. But they made a lot of them. And we never lost. We never lost.
